prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The best thing of all is to take the enemy’s country whole and intact. My mother took my heart out. She banked it on top of her stove. It glowed white. She put it back in my chest. Tita knew that overseas workers often had affairs. He licked me and I pretended it pinged through my body like a swift idea That I wrote about and considered like a bell of good craftsmanship. He also knew that their kids ate better He said your belly is like a cat’s. He said with his bowl up to his chin More please. At night the fireflies come out. They flock to my window. I put my hands up against the screen. I think how fragile it is to be inside a house. They say I want permission I paint my face. I say—just take it. Easy. If equally matched, we can offer battle. If unequal in any way, we can flee from him. Deprived of their father while sustained by his wages. I thought a lot about walking around at night. By myself. Just to think. But I never did. I thought I could just flick a switch. When I was born, my mother and father gave me a gardenia like personal star. Don’t you hate it when someone apologizes all the time? It’s like they are not even sorry.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, She, Tita

outputs.L1:
The best thing of all is to take the enemy’s country whole and intact. My mother took out my heart and banked it atop her stove. It glowed white. Then she placed it back inside my chest.

Tita knew that overseas workers often had affairs. He licked me, and I pretended the sensation rang through my body like a swift idea—one I wrote about and contemplated like a finely crafted bell. He also knew that their children ate better.

He said, “Your belly is like a cat’s.” With his bowl raised to his chin, he said, “More, please.”

At night, the fireflies emerge. They flock to my window. I press my hands against the screen and think how fragile it is to be inside a house.

They say, “I want permission.” I paint my face. I say, “Just take it. Easy.”

If equally matched, we can offer battle. If unequal in any way, we can flee from him.

Deprived of their father, yet sustained by his wages.

I often thought about walking around alone at night, just to think. But I never did. I thought I could simply flick a switch.

When I was born, my mother and father gave me a gardenia, like a personal star.

Don’t you hate it when someone apologizes all the time? It is as though they are not even sorry.
outputs.L2: Above all, the ideal outcome is to seize the enemy’s land without damaging it. My mother removed my heart and set it on her stove, where it burned bright white. Then she returned it to my chest. Tita understood that people working abroad frequently became involved in affairs. He ran his tongue over me, and I imagined the sensation flashing through my body like a sudden thought—something I later wrote about and examined like a finely made bell. He knew, too, that their children were better fed. He told me my stomach resembled a cat’s. Holding his bowl beneath his chin, he asked for more. After dark, fireflies gather outside my window. I press my palms against the screen and consider how little protection a house truly offers. They claim I am seeking permission. I color my face and answer, “Go ahead and take it. No trouble.” When our strength equals the enemy’s, we can engage in combat; if we are outmatched in any respect, we can retreat. Their father was absent, but his earnings continued to support them. Often, I imagined wandering alone at night simply to think, though I never actually did it. I believed it might be as simple as flipping a switch. At my birth, my parents gave me a gardenia that was like a star belonging only to me. Isn’t it irritating when a person keeps apologizing? Their constant apologies make them seem insincere.
outputs.L3:
The text juxtaposes different ways of responding to an enemy: conquering, fighting, or fleeing. These alternatives suggest more than military strategy; they represent competing approaches to fear, conflict, and survival. Victory may require domination, resistance may demand sacrifice, and escape may offer safety at the cost of surrender or displacement.

Against this strategic language, the image of a mother removing a heart, warming it, and placing it back introduces a surreal form of intimate care. Her action transforms emotional pain into something physical that can be held, protected, and restored. The scene suggests that maternal love possesses a healing power, even when that healing is unsettling or incomplete.

The text also explores the consequences of overseas labor. Working abroad allows a father to provide financial support for his children, but his income cannot compensate for his absence. The family survives materially while being deprived of his daily presence, affection, and guidance. Distance further places relationships under strain, creating suspicion and the possibility of infidelity. Economic sacrifice therefore becomes emotionally ambiguous: it protects the family while simultaneously threatening its unity.

Images of desire, fireflies, and nighttime solitude deepen this sense of uncertainty. Fireflies briefly illuminate the darkness, evoking fragile hope, fleeting attraction, or a freedom that can be imagined but not fully realized. The speaker’s solitude creates an atmosphere of vulnerability and confinement, as though the surrounding darkness reflects both physical isolation and emotional restriction.

Ultimately, the speaker reflects on identity and belonging within the family. Questions of who one is, what one owes to others, and whether one has permission to choose a different life remain unresolved. Repeated apologies offer little comfort because words lose meaning when they are not accompanied by change. The text thus presents family love as both sustaining and painful, shaped by care, absence, obligation, longing, and the difficult search for personal freedom.
outputs.L4:
Structured as a fragmented, poetic collage, the text moves rapidly between scenes of war planning, migrant labor, family recollection, sexual intimacy, and domestic unease. Its shifting voices resist a single, stable perspective. Instead, commands, memories, confessions, and dreamlike images overlap, suggesting that public violence and private experience cannot be neatly separated. Military strategy enters the language of the home, while ordinary gestures—working, eating, touching, remembering—are shadowed by displacement and danger.

Absence becomes one of the work’s central forces. Missing relatives, distant lovers, abandoned homes, and uncertain futures shape the lives of those who remain. Migrant labor is presented not simply as economic necessity but as a condition of estrangement, in which survival requires separation from family, language, and place. Family memories offer moments of connection, yet they also transmit unresolved fear. The past persists through inherited habits and silences, making later generations carry anxieties they did not create.

The treatment of sexuality likewise combines tenderness with vulnerability. Intimacy may offer refuge, but it is never fully protected from unequal power, loss, or the threat of intrusion. Bodies become sites where desire, control, labor, and violence converge. Surreal imagery intensifies this uncertainty: domestic objects appear strange or menacing, familiar spaces become unstable, and the boundary between memory and immediate danger begins to dissolve.

Through these juxtapositions, the collage portrays safety as temporary and belonging as fragile. Home is not necessarily a secure location; it may be a remembered place, a threatened space, or a relationship that can disappear. The text ultimately suggests that intimacy and survival are formed under pressure—by political violence, economic precarity, inherited trauma, and the constant possibility of separation. Yet the act of remembering and speaking across these fractures also becomes a way of preserving connection, even when certainty and permanence remain impossible.
outputs.L5:
**The Story of Tita**

The village knew Tita as a quiet but courageous woman. She lived in a small house near the river, where she grew flowers and cared for injured animals. Every morning, Tita opened her door and welcomed whatever the day brought.

One afternoon, she found a frightened bird beneath an old tree. Its wing was hurt, so Tita gently carried it home. She fed it, kept it warm, and waited patiently for it to recover.

Several weeks later, the bird was strong enough to fly again. Tita released it beside the river and watched as it disappeared into the bright sky. She smiled, knowing that even a small act of kindness could give someone their freedom.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal prose poem by collaging fragments about war strategy, mothers, sexuality, migrant families, fireflies, and apology. Preserve the disjointed, dreamlike transitions.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the generals arrange blue pins around a bowl of milk. Their strategy is simple: persuade the river it has always wanted to be a road. Meanwhile, mothers fold the names of the missing into shirts too small for anyone living.

In the orchard, desire wears a red scarf and no shoes. It says, Touch me where the border used to be. It says, Every body is a country invented by weather. Behind the packinghouse, two lovers trade passports with their mouths, uncertain which hunger belongs to whom.

A family moves north beneath one umbrella: grandmother, father, three children, a photograph of a kitchen still smoking. They carry spoons, seeds, a key that opens only memory. At checkpoints they answer questions with other questions. What is your destination? The fireflies. How long will you remain? Until the dark forgives us.

Night deploys its small green lanterns. No commander can explain their formation. They flicker over trenches, over motel balconies, over the mother asleep upright on a bus, her hand resting on the feverish moon of her daughter’s forehead.

Orders arrive: advance, retreat, erase the bridge after crossing. But the bridge has learned the word mother and refuses to burn.

I am sorry, says the match to the forest.

I am sorry, says the map to the feet.

I am sorry, says the body, opening its borders in the dark.

No one knows whether the war has ended. Somewhere a general overturns the bowl, and milk runs across the table like a pale, unarmed country. Outside, migrant children cup fireflies in their palms, carrying brief homes that brighten only when released.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental cento that interweaves lines resembling *The Art of War* with intimate contemporary poetry about family, desire, overseas workers, and childhood.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Art of Returning**

Know the ground:  
the kitchen at 3 a.m.,  
my mother counting remittances  
beside a bowl of cooling rice.

Know the weather:  
my father’s voice delayed  
across nine hours of ocean,  
rain entering the call.

All warfare is based on distance.  
All desire, too—  
your shirt on the chair,  
your country locked inside a screen.

Where the road narrows,  
carry only what can survive inspection:  
a photograph, two addresses,  
the smell of a child’s hair.

My aunt slept beneath borrowed curtains  
in a city of glass.  
By day she raised another woman’s sons;  
at night she whispered our names  
as if checking a perimeter.

Do not besiege a walled city  
unless there is no alternative.  
Do not ask who built the wall  
while your brother is still outside.

In childhood we fought with guava branches,  
declared the laundry line a border,  
made prisoners kneel in the dust  
then freed them when called to supper.

The victorious general calculates.  
My mother calculated school shoes,  
medicine, the price of pork,  
how many birthdays a body can miss  
before absence becomes a relative.

Appear near when you are far away.  
Wave from the airport window.  
Send photographs beside foreign flowers.  
Say, I am eating well.  
Say, the cold is nothing.  
Say, soon.

At the river, strike before crossing—  
but I crossed into your bed unarmed,  
carrying the small white flag  
of my undershirt.

You touched the scar on my shoulder  
like reading an old campaign map.  
Here, I said, was the bicycle.  
Here, the mango tree.  
Here, the hand that let me fall.

Feed the army from the enemy’s fields.  
Feed the family from night shifts,  
from polished floors, from children  
who call someone else Mama  
before sleep.

A good commander leaves an opening.  
So my grandmother kept the porch light burning  
for twenty-three years,  
though every moth in the province  
mistook it for the moon.

When surrounded, change shape.  
Become nurse, nanny, sailor, bride.  
Become the accent they can understand.  
Hide your first language  
under your tongue like a blade.

There are roads not to be followed.  
Still, we followed them:  
to departures, to contracts,  
to rooms where eight women dreamed  
in eight dialects of home.

The deepest strategy is tenderness—  
to peel an orange for the feverish,  
to send money without mentioning hunger,  
to forgive the child  
who no longer recognizes your face.

Know yourself.  
Know the one waiting.  
Know that neither remains still.

At dawn the general counts the living.  
My mother counts plates.  
One for each body in the house,  
one for the sea,  
one for whoever is coming back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a fragmented literary passage assembled from unrelated quotations, shifting abruptly between military aphorisms, magical realism, domestic memories, and reflections on loneliness.
counterfactuals.output:
“Never fortify the hill you cannot remember,” the general wrote in the margin of a cookbook.

At noon, yellow moths poured from the church bell, each carrying a tiny blue flame. No one remarked on it except the butcher, who removed his hat and whispered, “The dead have learned the road home.”

My mother kept buttons in a chipped porcelain cup. On winter evenings she spilled them across the table and sorted them by color, as if preparing uniforms for a miniature, peaceful army. “A clean kitchen,” she used to say, “is only a battlefield after the witnesses have gone.”

Advance before dawn.  
Count the bridges.  
Trust no map that shows the sea asleep.

For seven years the village well returned whatever was dropped into it: coins, wedding rings, a soldier’s left boot, three apologies folded into paper boats. Then one August it began returning snow.

I remember the smell of onions browning in butter, my father’s wet coat beside the stove, the small clock coughing itself toward midnight. Someone had left a glass of milk on the windowsill. By morning it was full of stars.

“Loneliness is not an empty room,” said the woman on the last train. “It is a room in which every object knows your name.”

Hold the line.  
Burn the letters.  
If surrounded, become the weather.

We slept beneath a roof that dreamed aloud. It muttered of red cavalry, migrating houses, and a river that refused to reach the ocean because it had fallen in love with a bridge. In the morning, dust covered the bread.

My sister called from a city I had never visited. Behind her voice, dishes clattered, a dog barked, and someone laughed as though the world had not ended.

“The first casualty is always the lamp left burning.”

Years later, alone at the kitchen table, I opened my mother’s cup. The buttons were warm. One of them beat softly against my palm, like a heart too small to belong to anyone, and from the darkened hallway came the measured sound of troops withdrawing through snow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you make a found poem using mixed source material? Include Sun Tzu-style tactical advice, a glowing heart placed on a stove, an absent migrant father, nighttime fireflies, and someone who apologizes too much.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Instructions for Crossing**

Know the ground before you enter it.  
Leave one road open  
for whatever must flee.

On the stove, a glowing heart—  
low flame, blue ring,  
its small red chambers simmering.

Father has crossed another border.  
His chair keeps its silence.  
His last message says: *Soon,*  
a country with no map.

Outside, fireflies signal  
from the dark grass:  
advance, vanish, advance.

I’m sorry, says the child  
to the cup, to the door,  
to the empty plate.

Do not strike where grief is strongest.  
Wait until it moves.  
Travel light.

I’m sorry, the child says again,  
lifting the heart from the heat  
with both hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce one paragraph of avant-garde prose poetry with no explanation or title. Let multiple voices and narratives collide, retaining irregular grammar, repetition, and emotionally charged images of bodies, houses, food, war, and family.
counterfactuals.output: Mother says the house is hungry, feed it a door, feed it the blue knuckles of winter; no, says the soldier under the table, houses eat sons, I have seen their chimneys chewing flags. We pass the bread hand to hand to hand until it becomes a small warm animal, until Father returns without his face and whispers I am home, I am home, though the walls deny him in six languages. In the kitchen my sister salts her wrists, laughing red laughter, while the radio counts backward through a city of spoons, tanks, teeth; somebody is boiling the photographs, somebody cries don’t waste the broth. I was born here, says the ceiling. I was buried here, says the child in my mouth. Outside, the war drags its metal wedding dress through the orchard and every apple opens an eye. Eat, Grandma commands, eat before they come, but they have come, they are always coming, wearing our coats, carrying our names like rifles, and the house keeps opening, opening—room after room after wound—while we sit at the long table, chewing smoke, calling each other darling, traitor, darling, more, more, more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
